strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem (reactive dance generation) with a well-motivated hierarchical/multi-scale design grounded in dance theory insights.
GRFSQ is a reasonable technical contribution, combining grouped and residual FSQ to provide multi-scale disentangled motion representation without codebook collapse issues of VQ-VAE.

BLC (block causal masking + periodic positional encoding) is a sensible and practically motivated solution to error accumulation in long-sequence generation, and the ablations (Table 3) show it has clear impact.
LDCFG is a novel and interesting extension of classifier-free guidance to hierarchical latent scales, enabling fine-grained fidelity-diversity control, supported by systematic ablations (Table 4).

Extensive ablation studies are provided covering representation capacity, progressive masking, residual layer count, BLC/dense sliding window, and LDCFG configurations, giving good insight into design choices.
Quantitative results on DD100 show clear improvements over Duolando and InterGen baselines across most metrics, and a user study supports perceptual superiority.
weaknesses: Evaluation is conducted on a single, relatively small dataset (DD100, only 1.95 hours), raising concerns about generalizability of the claimed state-of-the-art results; no cross-dataset validation is provided.

Only two baselines (Duolando, InterGen) are compared, and other cited duet-specific methods (ReMoS, RegenNet, DanY) mentioned in related work are not included as baselines, despite being directly relevant competitors.

The user study is very small (15 participants, 15 video pairs) and lacks statistical rigor (no significance testing, confidence intervals, or details on participant expertise), limiting confidence in perceptual claims.

Long-term coherence claims (a central motivation of the paper) are not directly validated with long-sequence-specific metrics or experiments beyond a proxy ablation; the paper itself admits the DD100 dataset's sequence length constraint prevents fully demonstrating BLC's benefit on genuinely long sequences, undermining the core contribution.

Some quantitative results appear inconsistent or under-explained — e.g., BAS interpretation seems ambiguous since GT itself does not have the highest BAS, making it hard to judge whether ReactDance's lower BAS is actually better or worse.

Missing details on statistical significance/variance across runs for reported metrics, and no computational efficiency/runtime comparisons despite claims of enabling 'efficient parallel generation' via BLC.

LDCFG improvement is demonstrated via manual tuning of scale-specific guidance weights on a single metric (FIDcd) with no principled or automated method to select these weights, limiting practical usability.

Some claims (e.g., 'firstly introduce GRFSQ') may overstate novelty since GRFSQ is essentially a combination of two existing techniques (FSQ and HiFi-Codec-style grouped-residual quantization), making the technical delta somewhat incremental.
Qualitative results (Fig. 5) provide only sparse static snapshots without accompanying video demonstrations, making it hard to assess actual temporal coherence and interaction quality claims.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (reactive dance generation) and identifies three plausible limitations (local interaction perception, temporal drift, quantization instability) that are reasonably grounded in dance-theory literature.

The GRFSQ representation, combining group and residual FSQ into a hierarchical, disentangled motion codec, is a sensible extension over VQ-VAE/HiFi-Codec style approaches and the progressive masking scheme for enabling scale-decoupled control is a reasonable technical idea.

The ablation studies (Tables 2-4) are relatively extensive, covering representation capacity, masking strategy, residual depth, BLC/dense sliding window, and LDCFG scale configurations, which helps illuminate the internal behavior of the proposed components.

Quantitative results on FIDk/FIDg/FIDcd show clear improvement over the two chosen baselines (Duolando, InterGen), and the qualitative figure suggests visibly more plausible interactions than at least one baseline.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single, small dataset (DD100, ~2 hours) with no cross-dataset validation, limiting confidence in generalizability of the reported SOTA claims.

Only two baselines are compared (Duolando and the not-RDG-specific InterGen, awkwardly adapted with padding/truncation), while several duet-specific methods explicitly discussed in the related work (e.g., ReMoS, RegenNet, DanY) are never empirically compared against, despite being readily citable competitors.

The core motivation of the paper is long-term/long-sequence coherence (L2), yet there is no quantitative experiment that varies generation length and reports how metrics (e.g., FID, coherence, drift) degrade over time; the BLC ablation appears to be run on the same short (8s) clips used for training, which does not directly validate the claimed long-term coherence benefit.

Diversity metrics (Divk, Divg, Divcd) are consistently lower for ReactDance than for both ground truth and the baselines, and this trade-off is not discussed or analyzed anywhere in the paper, despite diversity being one of the headline metrics reported.

The BAS (beat alignment) metric for ReactDance (0.1944) is lower than both baselines (0.2089, 0.2470) and further from ground truth in the opposite direction than one would expect if higorder alignment were improved; the paper does not explain or contextualize this counter-intuitive result.

The user study is very small (15 participants, 15 video pairs total), lacks any statistical significance testing, and does not report the breakdown/methodology in enough detail (e.g., whether comparisons were pairwise per video or aggregated), making the 'Wins' percentages hard to trust.
No inference-time or computational efficiency comparison is provided despite claims that BLC enables 'efficient parallel generation' as a key benefit over autoregressive baselines.

Notation is reused confusingly (e.g., R denotes both the number of residual FSQ layers and appears again as parameter counts in the implementation section, 'R=62.8M parameters'), and several passages have grammatical/typographical errors, reducing overall clarity and polish.

No code, model, or data-processing scripts are mentioned as being released, and enough implementation detail (e.g., full network architecture, exact hyperparameters beyond a few) is missing to make the work easily reproducible.

The paper's ablations do not include a direct comparison to non-hierarchical, single-scale FSQ (only to VQ-VAE), leaving open whether gains stem from FSQ itself versus the proposed group-residual hierarchy.
Limitations section is generic and does not address the more fundamental issues above (diversity trade-off, limited baselines, lack of direct long-sequence quantitative validation).

strengths: Well-motivated design grounded in dance theory, identifying three concrete limitations (L1-L3) of existing RDG methods and mapping each to a specific technical solution (GRFSQ, BLC, LDCFG).

GRFSQ is a reasonable and effective adaptation combining Finite Scalar Quantization with grouped residual structure and a novel progressive/dual-phase masking strategy, avoiding codebook collapse while enabling coarse-to-fine controllable decoding.

BLC mechanism (block-diagonal causal masking + periodic positional encoding + dense sliding window training) is a sensible solution to the well-known train/inference length mismatch problem in long sequence generation.

LDCFG is a novel and useful extension of classifier-free guidance that exploits the hierarchical GRFSQ representation to allow scale-specific fidelity-diversity control, with quantitative evidence of its benefit over uniform CFG scaling.

Extensive and well-organized ablation studies (Tables 2-4) individually validate each proposed component (GRFSQ vs VQ-VAE, PM on/off, residual layer count, BLC on/off, dense SW on/off, LDCFG scale settings with/without PM), giving good insight into why the method works.
Reports state-of-the-art quantitative results against Duolando and InterGen on DD100 across solo, interactive, and music-alignment metrics, plus a user study showing preference for ReactDance.
weaknesses: Evaluation is conducted on a single, relatively small dataset (DD100, 1.95 hours), raising concerns about generalization of the reported gains to other duet dance datasets or genres.

Only two baselines (Duolando, InterGen) are compared quantitatively despite the paper citing several other relevant duet-specific methods (ReMoS, RegenNet, Dance-with-You) that are not benchmarked, weakening the strength of the SOTA claim.

The InterGen baseline adaptation (forcing fixed 2066-frame windows via padding/truncation) seems suboptimal and produces extreme outlier metrics (e.g., FIDcd=346), which may make the comparison less fair/convincing rather than demonstrating a genuine architectural advantage.
The user study is small-scale (15 participants, 15 video pairs), limiting the statistical robustness of the perceptual quality claims.

No code, pretrained models, or dataset splits release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility given the many implementation details (masking rates, scaling factors, learning rate schedules) that could materially affect results.

The individual technical ingredients (FSQ, grouped residual quantization à la HiFi-Codec, classifier-free guidance, block-causal masking) are largely borrowed from prior work in adjacent domains; the core novelty lies mainly in their combination and adaptation to RDG rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

Limited discussion of computational cost, inference speed, and scalability (training reportedly takes multiple days on a single GPU per stage), which is relevant for practical deployment of a two-stage pipeline.

The claimed connection between L2 (temporal drift) and diffusion-based generation is somewhat underexplained, since the described problem (error accumulation) is more characteristic of autoregressive generation; the paper does not clearly justify why a similar issue arises in the parallel/block diffusion setting beyond position-encoding mismatch.

strengths: Addresses two well-motivated and understudied challenges in reactive dance generation (RDG): fine-grained spatial interaction modeling and long-term temporal coherence, with a coherent narrative connecting them to dance-theoretic principles.

The Hierarchical Finite Scalar Quantization (HFSQ) representation is a reasonable technical contribution that combines FSQ's stability with grouped residual quantization to disentangle coarse and fine motion semantics, and the ablation (Table 2, Fig. 6-7) shows clear quantitative and qualitative benefits over a comparable RVQ-VAE baseline.

Blockwise Local Context (BLC) sampling is a practical and efficient alternative to autoregressive/inpainting-based long-sequence generation, achieving both better coherence metrics (FIDcd, BED) and much lower inference time (AITS) compared to baselines and ablated variants.

Extensive empirical evaluation: comparisons against 5 adapted SOTA baselines across solo, interactive, alignment, and efficiency metrics, plus ablations for each major component (HFSQ, progressive masking, DSW/BLC, LDCFG) and a user study on long-form sequences (>60s).

Layer-Decoupled Classifier-Free Guidance (LDCFG) is a novel and intuitive extension of CFG to hierarchical latents, with quantitative trade-off analysis (Table 4) and qualitative demonstration of body-part-specific artistic control (Fig. 8).
The paper reports strong quantitative improvements over baselines (e.g., FIDk 5.57 vs next best 14.65, FIDcd 14.17 vs 17.49) and consistent user study preference across all three criteria.
weaknesses: Evaluation is conducted on a single dataset (DD100, only 1.95 hours), raising concerns about generalizability of the claimed improvements to other duet/dance datasets or domains; no cross-dataset validation is provided.

Baselines are adapted (often substantially re-engineered) versions of methods designed for different tasks (e.g., GestureLSM for co-speech gesture, InterGen for text-to-interaction, TCDiff for group dance), which raises questions about whether these adaptations were optimally tuned, potentially inflating the performance gap versus ReactDance.

No reported statistical significance testing or variance/error bars across multiple runs/seeds for the main quantitative comparisons in Table 1, weakening confidence in the observed margins, especially for closely competitive metrics like Divk/Divg where ReactDance is not always best.

The user study is relatively small (20 participants, 15 comparisons each) and lacks detail on how baselines were selected for each comparison, randomization, or inter-rater agreement, limiting the reliability of the subjective evaluation.

The claimed 'periodic causal masking' and DSW training conceptually resemble streaming/causal techniques already explored in works like MotionStreamer, and the novelty of BLC over such prior parallel/blockwise generation strategies is not sufficiently contrasted with direct empirical comparison to closely related long-sequence generation baselines (e.g., MotionStreamer or Lodge) on this task.

Limitations acknowledge lack of semantic interpretability of HFSQ hierarchy levels and omission of hand/finger motion, but do not discuss potential failure cases of the BLC block-diagonal masking (e.g., abrupt content changes across block boundaries in highly dynamic music) or robustness to leader motions far outside training distribution.

Given only two residual quantization levels (R=2) are used in the final architecture, the notion of a rich 'hierarchical' multi-scale representation is somewhat modest, and it's unclear how the method would scale with more residual levels or how sensitive results are to this choice beyond a single ablation row.

AITS reported is only 1.75s but details on how this compares fairly to baselines' inference lengths, and whether it is measured per fixed sequence length or per typical test sequence, are not entirely clear, limiting reproducibility of the efficiency claim.

strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated and relatively under-explored problem (reactive dance generation) and clearly articulates two concrete technical gaps: fine-grained spatial interaction and long-term temporal coherence.

The overall system design is coherent: HFSQ provides a structured coarse-to-fine latent space, BLC provides an efficient non-autoregressive long-sequence sampling strategy, and LDCFG extends classifier-free guidance to operate per-scale — these three pieces fit together logically within a single diffusion pipeline.

Extensive ablation studies are provided for each major component (HFSQ vs RVQ-VAE, progressive masking, dense sliding window stride, periodic positional encoding/causal masking, and LDCFG weight sweeps), with both quantitative and qualitative (visual) support.

Quantitative results on DD100 show sizeable improvements over multiple adapted SOTA baselines across solo motion quality, interaction quality, music alignment, and especially inference efficiency (AITS of 1.75s vs 2.9–5.2s for others).

A user study with 20 participants and standard motion-generation metrics (FID variants, MPJPE/MPJVE, BAS, BED) is included, along with qualitative figures illustrating specific failure modes of baselines (jitter collapse, uncoordinated interaction, overrotation) that the proposed method avoids.
weaknesses: All quantitative experiments are conducted on a single, fairly small dataset (DD100, 1.95 hours), so there is no evidence of the method's generalization to other duet/interaction motion datasets or genres; this substantially weakens claims of broad significance and robustness.

Individual technical components are largely incremental recombinations of existing ideas: FSQ (Mentzer et al.) plus grouped residual quantization from neural audio codecs (Yang et al., HiFi-Codec) for HFSQ, dense/overlapping sliding-window training and periodic/causal masking for BLC (conceptually close to prior streaming/chunked generation strategies), and CFG applied independently per hierarchical scale for LDCFG — the paper does not clearly demonstrate why these combinations are non-obvious or uniquely necessary for RDG versus other motion-generation tasks.

Several baseline numbers look implausibly poor (e.g., EDGE FIDcd of 1523, TCDiff FIDcd of 1472) compared to the proposed method's 14.17, raising concerns about whether baseline adaptations were properly tuned/optimized for the RDG task rather than being handicapped by ad hoc modifications, which would inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

The paper claims strong 'long-term temporal coherence' as a central contribution, but no coherence-vs-sequence-length curve or degradation analysis is shown (e.g., FID or drift as a function of generated sequence length) to substantiate this claim beyond aggregate metrics computed over long test sequences and a qualitative >60s claim.

The ablation table for dense sliding window strides (s=16, s=64) omits AITS values entirely, making it impossible to assess whether the efficiency gains are tied specifically to stride choice or to the BLC mechanism as a whole.

The choice of R=2 residual quantization layers is asserted as 'sufficient' without an ablation varying R (e.g., R=1 vs R=3), so the necessity of the hierarchical depth itself is not empirically justified.
No reported variance/confidence intervals for the main results table or the user study, and no discussion of statistical significance, limiting confidence in the reported margins over baselines.

The framing around 'dance theory' principles (hierarchical motion composition, modular temporal coherence) is largely rhetorical/motivational and not rigorously connected to the technical design choices beyond providing intuitive justification.

No code or model release is mentioned, and several implementation details (e.g., exact adaptation procedures for baselines, group size G, block size W) are not fully specified in the main text, raising reproducibility concerns.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation that identifies two concrete gaps in reactive dance generation (fine-grained spatial interaction and long-term temporal coherence) and grounds the proposed solutions in dance-theoretic principles.

Technically coherent framework: HFSQ combines FSQ stability with hierarchical/grouped residual quantization to avoid codebook collapse while enabling coarse-to-fine disentanglement, and BLC provides an efficient non-autoregressive alternative to slow/error-prone autoregressive long-sequence generation.

Strong empirical results: ReactDance clearly outperforms multiple adapted SOTA baselines (GestureLSM, EDGE, TCDiff, InterGen, Duolando) across solo, interaction, and alignment metrics, while also being the fastest at inference (AITS 1.75s vs 2.9-5.2s for baselines).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of HFSQ vs RVQ-VAE, progressive masking, dense sliding window training, and periodic positional encoding/causal masking, each supported by both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations.
LDCFG offers an interesting and practically useful mechanism for independent control over coarse/fine motion semantics, with a small sweep showing sensible fidelity-diversity trade-offs.
Includes a user study (20 participants) corroborating the quantitative claims about naturalness, music alignment, and interaction coordination for long-form sequences.
Clear writing and figures that make the pipeline (Fig. 2, 4) reasonably easy to follow.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single, relatively small dataset (DD100, 1.95 hours); there is no cross-dataset or out-of-domain evaluation to establish generalization of the hierarchical representation or BLC sampling.

Most baselines are not native reactive-dance models and had to be substantially modified (encoder swaps, architecture changes) by the authors; the quality/fairness of these adaptations is hard to verify and could bias the comparison in the proposed method's favor.

The technical novelty is largely a combination of existing components (FSQ, grouped/hierarchical residual quantization inspired by audio codecs, sliding-window training, periodic positional encoding/causal masking for parallel decoding, and layer-wise CFG) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper would benefit from more explicit discussion of what is genuinely novel versus adapted from prior audio/motion work.

Ablations for HFSQ only compare against a single alternative (RVQ-VAE); other reasonable baselines (e.g., plain VQ-VAE, single-scale FSQ, different R/G configurations) are not explored, limiting insight into design choices such as why R=2 is sufficient.

Block size W and sliding stride m are fixed in the main experiments; only two additional strides (16, 64) are tested in the ablation, leaving the sensitivity of BLC to these key hyperparameters largely unexplored.

No code or public release is mentioned, and several implementation details (e.g., exact architecture of the Transformer denoiser, FSQ level configuration, group count G) are only partially specified, which may hinder reproducibility.

The paper does not report failure cases or limitations of ReactDance itself beyond a brief mention of missing semantic interpretability and finger motion, making it hard to gauge robustness under harder duet interactions (e.g., contact-heavy partnering).

Reported metrics are computed on very long test sequences (avg. 2066 frames); it's unclear how metrics like FID/BAS are aggregated over such long sequences and whether this could introduce measurement artifacts not present in standard shorter-clip evaluations used by prior work.

strengths: Addresses two genuinely important and under-addressed problems in reactive dance generation: fine-grained spatial interaction fidelity and long-term temporal coherence.

The HFSQ representation (grouped residual FSQ) is a reasonable and well-motivated combination of FSQ stability with hierarchical/residual structure, and the paper provides a clear frequency-based interpretation of coarse vs. fine layers.

BLC (periodic causal masking + phase-aligned positional encoding + dense sliding-window training) is an interesting non-autoregressive approach to long-sequence generation that reports large efficiency gains (1.75s vs. 2.9-5.2s for baselines) while apparently avoiding autoregressive drift.

Extensive experimental section: many ablations (HFSQ vs RVQ-VAE vs VAE, progressive masking, DSW stride sweep including a fine-grained 6-point sweep, residual stage count R, LDCFG guidance weights), a user study, qualitative comparisons, and appendix analyses (hand motion, role-swapping, zero-shot generalization to FineDance, conditioning signal ablation).
Strong quantitative improvements over multiple retrained SOTA baselines across most solo, interaction, and efficiency metrics on DD100.
Reasonably clear method exposition with figures illustrating the pipeline, HFSQ encoding/decoding, and masking strategies.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely a careful engineering combination of existing techniques (FSQ, residual/grouped quantization inspired by neural audio codecs, sliding-window training, periodic positional encoding/causal masking, layer-wise CFG) rather than a fundamentally new representation or sampling paradigm; each individual component has clear precedent in prior work.

Evaluation is conducted on a single primary dataset (DD100); while a zero-shot generalization experiment on FineDance is included in the appendix, it is qualitative only (no quantitative metrics), limiting confidence in generalization claims.

Baselines were substantially modified/adapted by the authors for the RDG task (e.g., swapping text encoders for music/motion encoders); such re-implementations risk being suboptimal relative to the original methods' designs, which could inflate the apparent margin of improvement (e.g., FID gaps of 5x-20x seem unusually large and warrant scrutiny or independent verification).

Mixed metric results are somewhat underexplained: Duolando outperforms ReactDance on some diversity/velocity metrics (Divk, Divg, MPJVE) and BAS is not uniformly best, but the analysis focuses mostly on where ReactDance wins.

No code/data release is mentioned in the main text, and reproducibility of exact hyperparameters (e.g., DSW stride interacting with block size T, LDCFG dropout p=0.2) relies heavily on appendix details without a public repository, limiting practical reproducibility.

The paper introduces many interacting design choices (HFSQ, PM, DSW, BLC, LDCFG) but does not clearly isolate how much of the overall performance gain stems from each versus their combination in an end-to-end, statistically rigorous manner (e.g., no confidence intervals/error bars across seeds).

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence supports, e.g., 'solving the fundamental challenge of maintaining kinematic stability over extended durations' is an overreaching conclusion given a single-dataset, single-domain (dance) evaluation.

The R=2 vs R=3/4 trade-off analysis (Table 5) shows non-monotonic effects on generation FID that are attributed post-hoc to diffusion learning difficulty, without deeper theoretical or empirical justification for why exactly R=2 is optimal for this task in general.

strengths: The paper identifies two genuinely important and under-addressed problems in reactive dance generation (fine-grained spatial interaction and long-term temporal coherence) and proposes technically coherent solutions (HFSQ, BLC/DSW, LDCFG) that are reasonably well motivated by dance-theory analogies.

Extensive ablation studies are provided (HFSQ vs. RVQ-VAE vs. VAE, progressive masking, DSW stride sweep from s=1 to s=360, residual-stage scalability R=1..4, conditioning signal ablation, hand-motion analysis), which is unusually thorough and helps isolate the contribution of individual components.

Strong quantitative improvements over retrained baselines on nearly all reported metrics (FID, MPJPE/MPJVE, PFC, FIDcd, IPR, AITS), together with a user study and qualitative comparisons that support the coherence and quality claims.

The BLC/DSW mechanism for parallel long-sequence generation is a practically useful contribution, showing a large efficiency gain (1.75s AITS for >2000-frame sequences) versus slower autoregressive/iterative baselines.

Appendix contains additional generalization experiments (role swapping, zero-shot OOD on FineDance) that, if valid, strengthen claims about learning general interaction dynamics rather than memorizing dataset-specific patterns.
weaknesses: All quantitative results are on a single, fairly small dataset (DD100, 1.95 hours). Generalization claims rely mainly on qualitative video demonstrations on FineDance with no quantitative metrics, so robustness across datasets/domains is not rigorously established.

All baselines were reimplemented/adapted and retrained from scratch by the authors themselves (GestureLSM, EDGE, InterGen, TCDiff, Duolando), with no independent verification, official checkpoints, or sensitivity analysis of these adaptations; this raises fairness/tuning concerns, especially since some adaptations (e.g., replacing text encoders with music/motion encoders) are nontrivial and could disadvantage baselines not designed for this exact setup.

No code, model, or data release is mentioned anywhere in the paper, which is a significant reproducibility concern for a submission with this many interacting design choices (HFSQ grouping/residual stages, progressive masking schedule, BLC masking, DSW stride, LDCFG dropout probabilities, multiple loss weights).

Metric behavior is inconsistent with the paper's own narrative in places: e.g., BAS (which should be closer to Ground Truth, not necessarily lower) shows GestureLSM (0.1734) actually closer to GT (0.1791) than ReactDance (0.2031), yet this is not discussed or acknowledged, undermining confidence in the music-alignment claims.

The overall system is a complex pipeline with many interacting components (multi-stream leader/reactor representation, HFSQ with residual/group quantization, progressive masking, BLC periodic masking + phase-aligned positional encoding, DSW training, LDCFG with independent condition dropout); while ablations exist, they are largely piecemeal and it remains unclear how sensitive final performance is to the many hyperparameters (p=0.2 dropout, λ weights, block size T, stride m) or whether the gains are robust rather than the result of extensive tuning on this one dataset.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for any table, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (sometimes modest) margins over the second-best baseline on several metrics (e.g., Divk, Divg, BAS).

Some ablation claims are asserted with mechanistic explanations (e.g., 'Decoder as Kinematic Smoother', HFSQ providing a 'diffusion-friendly manifold') that are intuitively plausible but not rigorously demonstrated or theoretically justified beyond post-hoc narrative.

strengths: Addresses two concrete, well-motivated gaps in reactive dance generation (fine-grained spatial interaction and long-term temporal coherence), with a technically coherent solution (HFSQ + BLC + LDCFG) directly targeting each.

HFSQ representation is a reasonable and well-justified way to combine FSQ stability with hierarchical/residual structure, explicitly disentangling coarse posture from fine dynamics; the reconstruction and generation ablations (Table 2, Table 5) support the design choices, including a sensible analysis of the R=2 sweet spot.

BLC sampling is an elegant, practical solution to the long-sequence coherence problem, achieving both efficiency (1.75s for 2000+ frames) and coherence, with clear ablations isolating the roles of periodic masking/positional encoding and dense sliding-window training (Tables 3 and 6).

Extensive and unusually thorough empirical validation: strong quantitative gains over multiple adapted SOTA baselines across solo, interaction, alignment, and efficiency metrics; qualitative comparisons; a user study; and a rich appendix with ablations on conditioning signals, hand motion noise, role-swapping, and zero-shot OOD generalization to FineDance.
LDCFG provides an interesting, well-motivated mechanism for decoupled control over coarse/fine motion, with quantitative trade-off analysis and qualitative body-part control demonstrations.
Good writing and clear figures (Fig. 2 and 4) that make the pipeline easy to follow despite its many components.
weaknesses: All main experiments are conducted on a single, relatively small dataset (DD100, 1.95 hours); generalization claims rely mainly on qualitative OOD videos (FineDance) rather than quantitative OOD metrics, limiting confidence in broader applicability.

The overall contribution is largely a careful combination and adaptation of existing techniques (FSQ, residual/hierarchical quantization, periodic causal masking, sliding-window training, CFG) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; novelty is more in integration/engineering than in core algorithmic insight.

Baselines were substantially modified/retrained by the authors to fit the RDG setting (e.g., replacing text encoders with motion/music encoders), which introduces risk that suboptimal adaptation partly explains the large performance gaps rather than genuine architectural inferiority.

Minor inconsistencies in "outperforms on majority of metrics" claims are glossed over (e.g., ReactDance's IPR of 7.84 is actually worse than TCDiff's 7.58, and Divk/Divg/BAS are not uniformly best), which slightly overstates the completeness of the improvement.

The paper introduces many hyperparameters and interacting components (λ weights, masking probabilities, dropout rate, DSW stride, guidance weights per layer) without a full sensitivity or robustness analysis in the main text, raising some reproducibility/tuning-burden concerns.

The claimed "elimination" of temporal drift is asserted somewhat strongly given evaluation is limited to a fixed average test length (~2066 frames) rather than systematically stress-tested at increasing lengths to show where degradation, if any, eventually occurs.

Limitations acknowledged (lack of semantic interpretability of hierarchy levels, no finger motion) are real but somewhat narrowly scoped; broader discussion of failure modes (e.g., under what leader motion types the model still struggles) is largely deferred to appendix qualitative videos rather than rigorous quantitative failure analysis.
